explainer.heading: The story in brief
explainer.body: From R. K. Narayan’s “Swami and Friends”. Swaminathan hates Mondays after the freedom of the weekend. He rushes through homework, is pinched and scolded by his arithmetic teacher, enjoys the history period, and we meet his four special friends: Somu, Mani, Sankar and Samuel.
explainer.example: Set in the fictional South Indian town of Malgudi.
explainer.hook: Monday = work and discipline after delicious freedom.

explainer.heading: Morning at home
explainer.body: Swaminathan’s “room” is only a corner of his father’s dressing-room, with a table heaped with coat, cap, slate, ink-bottle and books. He has two hours for arithmetic (five profit-and-loss sums), English (copy a page and write dictionary meanings) and geography.

explainer.heading: In class
explainer.body: Fire-eyed Vedanayagam, the class teacher, takes arithmetic and drones monotonously. Swaminathan watches the Infant Standards and the 12.30 mail train on the embankment. Vedanayagam pinches his arm, crosses out all his sums, writes “Very Bad” and flings the notebook at him. History with D. Pillai is loved — he is kind, never frowns, and tells vivid stories of Vasco da Gama, Clive and Hastings. Scripture is the last period.

explainer.heading: The four friends
explainer.body: Somu — the confident monitor, chummy with teachers, “uncle of the class”. Mani — the Mighty Good-For-Nothing, tall, never does homework, bullies others; Swaminathan is proud to be his friend. Sankar — the most brilliant boy, solves problems in five minutes, scores around ninety per cent; some say he is a sycophant. Samuel — “the Pea” because of his size; ordinary, as weak in arithmetic as Swami, and the friend he feels closest to.

explainer.heading: Vocabulary
explainer.body: reluctant (unwilling), dismal (gloomy), monotonously (in a dull, unchanging way), reverie (daydream), scrutinising (examining closely), reprimand (scold). Negative prefixes: un- (unhappy, unkind), dis- (dislike, disagree, dishonest). Easily confused: lose/loose, quiet/quite.

explainer.heading: Grammar: gerunds and infinitives
explainer.body: Gerund = verb + -ing used as a noun (Swimming is fun). Some verbs take gerunds: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, keep. Some take infinitives (to + verb): want, decide, hope, plan, refuse. Some take both: like, love, start, begin.
explainer.example: Swami enjoyed watching the trains. / He decided to finish his sums.

explainer.heading: Writing & author
explainer.body: A newspaper report: headline, byline (reporter, place, date), opening paragraph answering who/what/when/where, details and quotes, passive voice and past tense, neutral tone. R. K. Narayan was a 20th-century Indian writer famous for stories set in Malgudi.

Why was Swaminathan proud of his friendship with Mani?
questions.model: Mani was feared by the whole class and even teachers did not trouble him. While others were scared of him, Swaminathan could call him “Mani” and pat him on the back.
points: Swami could treat him familiarly (call him Mani, pat his back)

questions.q: Write a short note on D. Pillai.
questions.model: D. Pillai was the history teacher, known for kindness and good humour. He never frowned or scolded the boys and taught history through vivid, detailed stories of people like Vasco da Gama and Clive, so the boys loved his class.
points: Taught history as vivid stories → boys loved it

questions.q: Compare the arithmetic and history periods and describe Swaminathan’s four friends briefly.
questions.model: Arithmetic with fire-eyed Vedanayagam was dull and frightening: he droned monotonously, pinched Swami, crossed out his sums and wrote “Very Bad”. History with kind D. Pillai was exciting as he told stories with rich detail. Swami’s friends: Somu, the calm, confident monitor; Mani, the strong, lazy bully; Sankar, the brilliant boy who scored ninety per cent; and Samuel “the Pea”, small and ordinary like Swami.
points: History: kind D. Pillai, story-like teaching
